claim: MedEinst: 5,383 paired medical cases (control vs trap with flipped evidence) across 49 diseases, 17 LLMs; frontier models have high accuracy but severe Bias Trap Rate (Einstellung-like lock-in on the typical diagnosis).
authors: Wenting Chen, Zhongrui Zhu, Guolin Huang, Wenxuan Wang
title: MedEinst: Benchmarking the Einstellung Effect in Medical LLMs through Counterfactual Differential Diagnosis
transfer: On open or diagnostic tasks, test whether the first answer still fits a changed fact: re-check the answer against one counterfactual cue.

claim: The earlier brief's '60.9% for one model' MedEinst figure was NOT confirmed on the abstract page; the abstract gives no per-model number. Treat that figure as unverified.
authors: Wenting Chen et al.
title: MedEinst
transfer: none (correction to earlier brief)

claim: PreFlect has agents critique and refine plans before acting, using planning errors distilled from past trajectories, plus dynamic re-planning; the abstract reports gains over reflection baselines but gives no numbers.
quote: a prospective reflection mechanism that shifts the paradigm from post hoc correction to pre-execution foresight
authors: Hanyu Wang, Yuanpu Cao, Lu Lin, Jinghui Chen
title: PreFlect: From Retrospective to Prospective Reflection in Large Language Model Agents
transfer: Pre-mortem step before costly actions, grounded in a ledger of past failure causes, not free-form doubt.

claim: Without external feedback, LLMs struggle to self-correct reasoning and sometimes get worse after trying.
quote: struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback
authors: Jie Huang, Xinyun Chen, Swaroop Mishra, Huaixiu Steven Zheng, Adams Wei Yu, Xinying Song, Denny Zhou
title: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
transfer: Any doubt or revise step needs an outside signal (run, test, differing input), never pure self-review.

claim: A critical survey finds no prior work shows successful self-correction using feedback from prompted LLMs except on unusually well-suited tasks; self-correction works with reliable external feedback or with large-scale fine-tuning.
quote: there is still no consensus on the question of when LLMs can correct their own mistakes
authors: Ryo Kamoi, Yusen Zhang, Nan Zhang, Jiawei Han, Rui Zhang
title: When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs
transfer: Gate the critic step on tool or checker feedback; skip prompt-only critique on single-answer tasks.

claim: GPT-4 is poor both at solving graph coloring and at verifying its own solutions; LLM self-critique loops do not help, and gains from iterative prompting appear because the correct answer is already among top-k completions that an external verifier can spot.
quote: seems largely irrelevant to the performance of iterative prompting
authors: Kaya Stechly, Matthew Marquez, Subbarao Kambhampati
title: GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong: An Analysis of Iterative Prompting for Reasoning Problems
transfer: Generate several candidates, then let an external verifier pick; do not rely on critique text.

claim: Multi-agent debate systems do not reliably beat self-consistency or ensembling over reasoning paths in a cost and accuracy benchmark; some improve with tuning, and adjusting agent agreement level can improve debate beyond non-debate protocols.
authors: Andries Smit, Paul Duckworth, Nathan Grinsztajn, Thomas D. Barrett, Arnu Pretorius
title: Should we be going MAD? A Look at Multi-Agent Debate Strategies for LLMs
transfer: Do not build a debate stage as the default; if used, tune agreement level and compare to self-consistency at equal tokens.

claim: Du et al. report that multiple model instances proposing, critiquing and revising over rounds improve math, strategy and factuality.
quote: significantly enhances mathematical and strategic reasoning across a number of tasks
authors: Yilun Du, Shuang Li, Antonio Torralba, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Igor Mordatch
title: Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
transfer: Argumentative theory in machine form; weigh against Smit et al. (b-07): gain may be sampling.

claim: LLMs tell their own outputs apart from others with non-trivial accuracy, fine-tuning shows a linear link between self-recognition and self-preference, and controlled experiments suggest the link is causal.
quote: self-preference, where an LLM evaluator scores its own outputs higher than others'
authors: Arjun Panickssery, Samuel R. Bowman, Shi Feng
title: LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
transfer: Strip authorship and shuffle order when a call judges candidates; prefer a judge from a different prompt or model.

claim: Errors of different LLMs are substantially correlated: across 350+ models, when two models are both wrong they give the same wrong answer about 60% of the time; larger models stay highly correlated.
quote: models agree 60% of the time when both models err
authors: Elliot Kim, Avi Garg, Kenny Peng, Nikhil Garg
title: Correlated Errors in Large Language Models
transfer: Agreement across samples (and even across models) is weak evidence of truth; do not use vote share alone as a trust gate.

claim: Verbalized LLM confidence is overconfident; consistency across multiple samples and human-inspired prompts reduce overconfidence; no single method wins, and all struggle on professional-knowledge tasks.
authors: Miao Xiong, Zhiyuan Hu, Xinyang Lu, Yifei Li, Jie Fu, Junxian He, Bryan Hooi
title: Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs
transfer: Trust gate (Kahneman-Klein style) cannot use stated confidence; use sample consistency plus checks, and accept it is imperfect.

claim: White-box confidence methods beat black-box ones only narrowly (AUROC range 0.522 to 0.605 reported); confidence-based failure prediction is weak.
authors: Xiong et al.
title: Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty?
transfer: Expect a confidence-based router to be weak; measure its AUROC on our own logged routes before relying on it.

claim: GPT-3-davinci-003 gave intuitive trap answers on 70-90% of cognitive reflection tasks (humans 55%); ChatGPT-3.5 15% and ChatGPT-4 0%, with correct answers 59% and 96%.
quote: ChatGPT models tend to engage in chain-of-thought reasoning
authors: Thilo Hagendorff, Sarah Fabi, Michal Kosinski
title: Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in large language models but disappeared in ChatGPT
n: 150 CRT tasks, 50 semantic illusions, 10 GPT models
transfer: Newer instruct models mostly escape classic intuition traps; do not add a slow-override step for known trap puzzles.

claim: Forcing ChatGPT to answer briefly barely changed its accuracy, so chain of thought does not fully explain its performance; the authors read this as well-developed intuition.
authors: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski
title: Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in large language models but disappeared in ChatGPT
transfer: On regular tasks the first fast answer is often already good: let the router skip deliberation when probes agree and a check passes.

claim: Meta-analysis of 100+ chain-of-thought papers plus 20 datasets on 14 models: CoT helps mainly on math and logic; on MMLU direct answering is nearly as good unless an equals sign is present.
quote: CoT gives strong performance benefits primarily on tasks involving math or logic
authors: Zayne Sprague, Fangcong Yin, Juan Diego Rodriguez, Dongwei Jiang, Manya Wadhwa, Prasann Singhal, Xinyu Zhao, Xi Ye, Kyle Mahowald, Greg Durrett
title: To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning
transfer: Route by task type: apply stepwise simulation only to symbolic or computational items; use direct answer elsewhere.

claim: Self-consistency (sample several reasoning paths, keep the most common answer) improved over greedy CoT: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-challenge +3.9 points.
quote: a complex reasoning problem typically admits multiple different ways of thinking
authors: Xuezhi Wang, Jason Wei, Dale Schuurmans, Quoc Le, Ed Chi, Sharan Narang, Aakanksha Chowdhery, Denny Zhou
title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
transfer: The baseline any expert-decision step must beat at equal tokens.

claim: A transformer trained on Stockfish action-values (270M params, no explicit search) reaches Lichess blitz rating 2895, about grandmaster level, and solves hard puzzles: strong pattern recognition (chunk-like) can replace search.
quote: perfect distillation is still beyond reach, thus making ChessBench well-suited for future research.
authors: Anian Ruoss, Gregoire Deletang, Sourabh Medapati, Jordi Grau-Moya, Li Kevin Wenliang, Elliot Catt, John Reid, Cannada A. Lewis, Joel Veness, Tim Genewein
title: Amortized Planning with Large-Scale Transformers: A Case Study on Chess
transfer: Supports recognition-first: in a trained domain the first pattern answer is strong; add search only where recognition is uncertain. Not a prompting result.

claim: Chain-of-thought explanations can be unfaithful: biasing features (e.g. correct answer always option A) cut accuracy by up to 36% across 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks (GPT-3.5, Claude 1.0) while explanations rarely mention the bias.
quote: CoT explanations can systematically misrepresent the true reason for a model's prediction.
authors: Miles Turpin, Julian Michael, Ethan Perez, Samuel R. Bowman
title: Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
transfer: Models rationalize (argumentative theory in machine form): a self-written justification is not evidence; verify by run, not by reading the reasoning.

claim: On syllogisms, larger PaLM 2 models reason more logically than smaller ones and than humans, yet still make systematic errors, some matching human biases (term order), some confident wrong conclusions.
authors: Tiwalayo Eisape, MH Tessler, Ishita Dasgupta, Fei Sha, Sjoerd van Steenkiste, Tal Linzen
title: A Systematic Comparison of Syllogistic Reasoning in Humans and Language Models
transfer: Mental-model counterexample step is untested as a prompt; model errors partly mirror human content effects, so keep a check outside the model.

claim: RULEBREAKERS: on cases where strict logic gives a conclusion humans reject by common sense, seven LLMs including GPT-4o reach only mediocre accuracy and apply rules too rigidly; the authors caution against pushing formal logic methods.
quote: most models, including GPT-4o, achieve mediocre accuracy on RULEBREAKERS
authors: Jason Chan, Robert Gaizauskas, Zhixue Zhao
title: RULEBREAKERS: Challenging LLMs at the Crossroads between Formal Logic and Human-like Reasoning
transfer: A counterexample or logic-check step can over-apply rules; pair it with a plausibility check against the given examples.
